items.title: The mid-life income cliff: laid off at 46-55, earn 25% less three years later
items.idea: Using Great Recession data, workers laid off at 46-55 were still earning about 25% less three years later, even after finding new jobs. In 2023-2026 data, 51.1% of all laid-off workers end up earning less, and that sample includes young workers who should be earning more. Their rule: by about 40, income you earn yourself should exceed your W-2 income, or at minimum replace a third of it.
items.angle: This is the labor-market version of duration risk. If AI cuts white-collar headcount at the 45-55 band first, consumption from the highest-earning cohort falls faster than the unemployment rate shows.
items.tweetA: 51.1% of laid-off workers earn less afterwards. For 46-55 year olds it's about 25% less, three years later. The unemployment rate tells you who has a job. It doesn't tell you the job pays 25% less. That's the AI layoff number to watch.
items.tweetB: Everyone diversifies their portfolio. Almost nobody diversifies the income that funds it. If your peak earning years are 40-49 and that is also when firms look for cheaper replacements, your biggest concentrated position is your employer.

charts.desc: Charts on post-layoff earnings by age cohort (Great Recession) and share of laid-off workers earning less (2023-26)

items.title: Banker, doctor and lawyer pay flat-to-down since 2010 while e-commerce sales rise 10%
items.idea: BowTiedBull argues pay for investment bankers, doctors and lawyers has been flat to down in real terms since about 2010, against strong inflation in high-quality housing. Meanwhile US e-commerce sales are up about 10% y/y, and Etsy alone moves about $10B a year. They frame it as: elite W-2 roles now lose to asset owners and small online sellers.
items.angle: If professional-class wages lag asset prices for 15 years, the political pressure moves to housing and asset taxes. It also helps explain the retail speculation in crypto and meme stocks.
items.tweetA: Doctor, lawyer and banker pay: flat since 2010. Good housing: not flat. That gap is why a 35-year-old professional buys 3x leveraged ETFs. Wages can't close it, so they're trying leverage.
items.tweetB: Everyone says AI will kill online side businesses. US e-commerce is up 10% y/y. The pressure is landing on salaried knowledge work, not on people who sell things.

items.title: Vanda: retail NVDA dip-buyers of Nov 16-20 averaged $148.40. The whole month is only back to breakeven
items.idea: Vanda's Viraj Patel ('The Last CUDAnce') estimates retail buying NVDA during Nov 16-20 entered at about $148.40. That was -15.4% by Friday and about +11% after Monday's 31% rally. The average retail position across all of November is only around breakeven, and retail has been selling other holdings to fund the trade, with growing leverage.
items.angle: With NVDA about -5% premarket (about $157), the Nov 16-20 cohort's cushion is already down from +11% to about +6%. Retail funding NVDA by selling other holdings explains why breadth outside AI is so poor.
items.tweetA: Retail's November NVDA cost basis is about breakeven. Monday's 31% rally only took them back to flat. Today NVDA is -5% premarket. Watch $148 on $NVDA: that's where the dip-buyers go from relieved to underwater again.
items.tweetB: The detail that matters: retail sold other stocks to buy $NVDA. So Monday's rally was a single-stock squeeze paid for by the rest of retail's portfolios. Meme stocks, crypto and small caps were the source of funds.

items.title: Houthis have hit Aramco HQ in Dhahran, Aramco's Riyadh tower and a PIF tower in five weeks
items.idea: Doomberg lists Houthi strikes on Aramco HQ in Dhahran (Oct 14, 'extensive damage'), the Aramco tower in Riyadh's financial district (Nov 8) and a PIF tower (Nov 19). Saudi-backed forces in Yemen are collapsing and the battle for Aden is approaching. Doomberg frames the outcome as existential for MBS.
items.angle: Three strikes on symbols of the Kingdom in 36 days, and oil is down to $80. The market prices Hormuz-Iran risk but not a Saudi internal-stability premium.
items.tweetA: Houthi missiles hit Aramco HQ on Oct 14, Aramco Riyadh on Nov 8 and the PIF tower on Nov 19. Brent is about $80 and falling. Either the market thinks Aden doesn't matter, or nobody is reading Yemen headlines.
items.tweetB: One strike a fortnight on symbolic Saudi targets, with the Aden front collapsing. The relevant question for oil vol isn't Hormuz. It's what Saudi spare capacity is worth if Riyadh itself is in range.

items.title: Is the gold drop forced Saudi selling? Doomberg backs PauloMacro's deposit-shortage thesis
items.idea: Doomberg quotes PauloMacro: the precious-metals drop isn't about the Fed or liquidity but about 'gold holders need cash, and urgently so'. He points at Saudi Arabia's equity market (KSA ETF), sovereign CDS and banks, with 'a clear deposit shortage'. Doomberg says 'we suspect he is right', citing rumours of a Saudi funding crisis hidden by censorship.
items.angle: If this is right, the gold dip is a sovereign liquidation (a seller who doesn't care about price), not a change in the macro view. That's usually a buying setup once the selling stops. Things to watch: KSA ETF, Saudi 5y CDS, SAIBOR-SOFR spread.
items.tweetA: Gold falling during a war and with inflation above target doesn't add up, unless a sovereign is selling for cash. Watch Saudi CDS and $KSA, not the Fed. If that's the seller, the low comes when they're done, not when the macro changes. $GLD
items.tweetB: Second-order effect of Hormuz: the Gulf state that can't ship as much oil still has to fund its budget. Gold is the most liquid asset it can sell. A war that should be bullish for gold can be bearish for it in the short run.

items.title: COP31 in Türkiye collapses, the first failed final agreement since Copenhagen 2009
items.idea: UN climate talks broke down with no final agreement. Oil producers led by Saudi Arabia and Russia blocked any mention of fossil fuels, and the EU and climate-vulnerable states rejected the weakened text. It's the first COP to fail on a final agreement since COP15 in 2009.
items.angle: Climate diplomacy failing when European energy is scarce makes EU climate policy harder to sustain politically. Watch EUA carbon prices and how fast EU ETS2 gets watered down.
items.tweetA: The first failed COP since 2009 happened the same winter Europe might run out of gas. Producers didn't need to win the argument. They just needed Europe to be short of energy while it was being made.
items.tweetB: Saudi Arabia and Russia blocked the word 'fossil fuels' from the COP31 text. With Houthis hitting Aramco and Ukraine hitting Russian refineries, the two biggest blockers are also the two most exposed to physical supply shocks.

items.title: Fed FEDS Note: a drop in LNG imports would leave EU gas storage nearly empty by spring
items.idea: A Fed Board FEDS Note published Friday projects EU gas inventories to June 2027. It finds Europe gets through an average winter, and a harsh one with stocks lower than it has ever tolerated, but 'a notable decline in LNG imports would leave storage nearly empty by the spring.' Melandri (Market House) puts storage at 56% vs a normal 88%, with temperatures 5-6°C below normal.
items.angle: It's unusual for the Fed to model another region's energy security. The scenario depends on LNG, and LNG depends on Qatar and Hormuz. TTF calendar spreads look cheap insurance.
items.tweetA: The Fed published a note on whether Europe runs out of gas. Base case: no. Weak spot: LNG imports. Where does a fifth of global LNG pass through? Hormuz. $TTF
items.tweetB: EU gas storage 56% vs 88% normal (Melandri), weather 5-6°C colder than usual, and the Fed modelling 'nearly empty by spring.' The euro is at 1.088 and falling. An energy shock isn't priced into EUR/USD yet.

items.title: An Anthropic mathematician claims a Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis, verified by computer code
items.idea: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a four-page note saying he completed a proof of the Riemann hypothesis with Claude. Instead of a traditional paper, he linked computer code he says verifies the result. Doomberg's point: four years from failing 'strawberry' to this. Mando Minutes separately reports 'Claude claims proof of VP ≠ VNP.'
items.angle: If machine-checked proofs hold up, AI's value moves from writing code to producing verifiable new knowledge, and the pricing power comes with it. Watch whether formal verification (Lean) becomes standard and how much compute labs give to math.
items.tweetA: Four years ago LLMs couldn't count the r's in strawberry. This week: a claimed machine-checked Riemann proof and a claimed VP ≠ VNP. Even if one fails review, AI is now being used on open research problems, not just to save labor.
items.tweetB: What matters about the Riemann claim isn't the result. It's that the proof is shipped as verification code instead of a paper. If proofs become executable, peer review becomes a compute problem, and it scales like one.

items.title: DXY rallies in risk-off and risk-on: 104.53 YTD high, testing 104.60, ahead of short-rate spreads
items.idea: The dollar rose during last week's tech liquidation, and then rose again on Monday's Nvidia rebound, to a YTD high of 104.53. Innes says the move has 'substantially outrun' short-term US rate differentials. It is testing 104.60 resistance in thin Thanksgiving liquidity, with month-end flows. Two explanations: unhedged foreign buying of US tech, or plain momentum-chasing.
items.angle: When the dollar rallies on both risk-off and risk-on, positioning is driving it. The setup for a reversal is Dec 9 FOMC / Dec 10 CPI base effects. For now, EM and gold have a strong dollar working against them.
items.tweetA: Tech crashes: buy dollars. Tech rips 6.5%: buy more dollars. When an asset rallies on both outcomes, positioning is doing the work, not the fundamentals. DXY 104.60 in Thanksgiving liquidity is a poor place to be adding. $DXY
items.tweetB: If Monday's dollar rally is foreigners buying US tech unhedged, then today's -5% NVDA premarket is a dollar story as well. The AI trade and the dollar are one crowded position now.

items.title: The 'Trump put' gives the Fed more room to hike: Williams won't rule out back-to-back hikes
items.idea: The NY Fed's Williams said inflation is too high and wouldn't rule out hikes at consecutive meetings, while saying an AI-sector deterioration would change his outlook. 2y yields +4bp on the equity bounce. Core PCE on Wednesday is expected to rise to 3.2% y/y from 3.1%. The offset: US gasoline is down about 14.5% since late September.
items.angle: The White House bailout of the equity market removed the Fed's reason to pause. A firm PCE plus a Dec 9 hike is the base case. A flatter curve and lower long-duration growth multiples follow.
items.tweetA: The White House put a floor under $NVDA. In doing so it removed the main thing stopping the Fed from hiking. That's why 2y yields rose on the rally. A put on stocks can mean a higher cost of money.
items.tweetB: Gasoline down 14.5% since September, core PCE expected to go up to 3.2%. Headline relief and core heat at once. The Fed has said it targets core, so cheaper gas won't prevent a December hike.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (FX Daily)
items.title: EUR/USD breaks 1.0880, but Innes says this is a dollar move, not a euro one
items.idea: EUR/USD fell below 1.0880 support on broad dollar demand, not on eurozone news. The euro's trade-weighted index is down about 3% over a year, which the ECB is likely to tolerate. German flash PMI beat slightly. Innes says a recovery above 1.0880 would mean the break was exaggerated by thin liquidity.
items.angle: Doomberg's EU gas scenario plus Melandri's 56% storage figure give a fundamental euro bear case the FX desk isn't citing yet. If 1.0880 holds as resistance, an energy shock would be the next leg.
items.tweetA: FX desks say the euro break below 1.0880 is 'just dollar strength.' Meanwhile EU gas storage is 56% vs 88% normal and the Fed is modelling empty tanks by spring. The euro-specific bear case hasn't been priced. $EURUSD
items.tweetB: The ECB doesn't mind a 3% weaker trade-weighted euro, and exporters like it. But it imports energy priced in dollars, so a weaker euro during a gas squeeze is a cost increase, not a stimulus.

items.title: Keysight: AI bookings 2.5x, orders +53% to $2.34B, third straight ~50% order quarter, and 6G doubled
items.idea: Keysight Q4 orders were a record $2.339B (+53% reported, +49% core), with book-to-bill 1.17. Revenue +41%, adjusted operating margin +950bp to 35.8%, adjusted EPS +89%. AI bookings were about 2.5x last year and the AI customer base nearly doubled, driven by 800G/1.6T transceiver ramps, early 3.2T research and hyperscaler workload emulation. The 6G business doubled. FY27 base case is 20% growth, and supply is 'the governor.' It trades at 19.3x BofA's FY27 EPS.
items.angle: Test-and-measurement is how optical speed upgrades show up in revenue before the volume does. Analysts raised EPS 10% and cut price targets, so the multiple compressed even as estimates rose.
items.tweetA: Keysight: AI bookings 2.5x, orders +53%, 3.2T already in research. Analysts raised EPS 10% and cut price targets. That's the AI picks-and-shovels trade at 19x forward. $KEYS
items.tweetB: Before any 1.6T or 3.2T optical link ships, someone pays to test it. Keysight's wireline growth was triple-digit. Speed upgrades show up in test budgets first. $KEYS $COHR $LITE

items.title: CrowdStrike buys Zscaler in an all-stock deal at 1.135 shares; ZS +17.7%
items.idea: CrowdStrike agreed to acquire Zscaler for 1.135 CRWD shares per ZS share. ZS rose 17.67% to $229.24, near deal value. It puts the two largest independent security platforms together (endpoint plus zero-trust network).
items.angle: An all-stock deal at this size, in a correction, means CRWD is using its stock as currency while it can. Read-through: pressure on PANW, Netskope and other SASE names to consolidate or partner.
items.tweetA: CrowdStrike paying in stock for Zscaler during a tech correction is a clue: management thinks its own stock is the expensive asset. In a downturn, companies that pay cash and companies that pay stock tell you different things. $CRWD $ZS
items.tweetB: Endpoint plus zero-trust in one company. $PANW now competes with a single platform that owns the agent and the network path. The rest of security will feel pressure to merge.

items.title: Big Moves: NVDA needs another ~40% to make holders from two months ago whole
items.idea: The author, writing personally, calls Huang's reinstatement a governance failure ('lying to his board... should be a governance third rail'), while admitting he profited through mutual funds. NVDA had fallen to the fourth-largest US stock before Monday's ~$1T rally put it back at #2, behind Apple. The board added a National Security and Export Control Committee and is hiring a chief compliance officer, and the independent investigation remains open.
items.angle: A 31% one-day gain still leaves NVDA about 40% below its high. Arithmetic: $165 × 1.4 ≈ $231. Holders who bought in the last two months still need a lot more upside.
items.tweetA: $NVDA up 31% in a day and still needs about 40% more to get back to where it was two months ago. That's what it looks like when a stock has fallen around 29% from its peak (165/231). One day of buying doesn't undo it.
items.tweetB: The board said it had 'no intention' to reinstate Jensen. Six days later it did so unanimously, citing 'input from senior levels of the US government.' The new compliance committee is there to reassure, but the board has already shown it can be overridden.

items.title: International Paper's DS Smith spin-off will be taxable for US shareholders, plus an LSE delisting
items.idea: IP fell 4.55% to $28.98 after approving the spin-off of its EMEA packaging business as DS Smith. The distribution is expected to be taxable to US holders, and IP plans to delist from the London Stock Exchange after separation.
items.angle: A taxable spin means US holders get a tax bill on the shares received. Expect forced selling of DS Smith by US accounts after the distribution, which is a classic spin-off setup.
items.tweetA: A taxable spin-off: you get DS Smith shares and a tax bill. Many US holders will sell the spin to pay it. After the distribution, look at DS Smith where US holders are forced sellers. $IP
items.tweetB: IP delisting from London after buying DS Smith is another blow to UK listings: a British company bought, split up, and its US parent leaving the LSE.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Citadel Securities' Nohshad Shah)
items.title: Citadel Securities' Shah: three AI risks: tighter macro, AI revenue economics, and politics
items.idea: In 'From Agentic to Agency Risks,' Nohshad Shah lists three connected vulnerabilities in the AI trade: a less supportive macro backdrop as the Fed leans against inflation; questions about how adoption and pricing turn into actual revenue; and political constraints that may decide how far and how fast AI is 'allowed' to go. He argues the tech correction may be signalling something about the wider economy that headline growth figures don't show yet. (Email is a teaser.)
items.angle: This is the third major desk (with GS Callahan and JPM's dropped bullish view) to frame Monday as a relief rally inside a regime change. The political risk is the new part, and Monday's White House intervention confirmed it can go either way.
items.tweetA: Citadel's new AI risk: 'agency risk.' Monday showed how it works. The White House can bring back a CEO, so it can also cap AI buildout through export rules, power permitting or labor politics. That risk goes both ways.
items.tweetB: Tighter Fed, uncertain AI revenue, political constraints. Monday's rally fixed none of them. It removed one person-specific risk at Nvidia. The three structural problems are still there.

items.title: Largest QQQ/XLK/SOX gap up ever, and NVDA's +$953bn is the largest single-day market-cap gain in history
items.idea: QQQ, XLK and SOX had their largest gap up ever. SPY's was its 5th largest and the biggest since Mar 24, 2020. 83% of S&P and 90% of NDX names closed up. NVDA posted its 4th-biggest % gain (the top one is its IPO day) and the largest one-day market-cap increase of any stock ever, $953bn. SOX had its 4th-biggest day in 32 years. Leaders were retail favourites, AI, high beta, bitcoin-sensitive names and momentum.
items.angle: Record gap-ups cluster near bear-market lows and inside bear-market rallies (2008, 2020, 2022). With NVDA -5% premarket the next day, the second day of the move is the tell.
items.tweetA: Largest gap up ever for $QQQ, $XLK and $SOX. Most of the previous record days happened inside bear markets, not at the start of bull markets. Today's -5% NVDA premarket is a test of which this is.
items.tweetB: $NVDA added $953bn in one day, more than the total market cap of all but about 10 companies. One CEO decision moved more value than most countries' stock markets are worth. That's concentration risk.

items.title: SixSigmaCapital: Monday looks like a counter-trend rally; bottoming checklist and index levels to watch
items.idea: SixSigmaCapital's chat-thread post argues 'yesterday's rally looks like a counter-trend rally for now,' and links a bottoming checklist and key index levels. (Email is only a link and one sentence; details are in the post.)
items.angle: This matches Melandri (bear market rally), Rosenberg (dead cat bounce) and Peter Brandt (V-bottom unproven). Few of today's sources treat Monday as the bottom.
items.tweetA: Count the views: Melandri says bear market rally. Rosenberg says dead cat. Brandt says V-bottom unproven. SixSigma says counter-trend. Steno says 1998. When almost everyone calls a record up-day a fake-out, I start to wonder whether the bearish consensus is the crowded side.
items.tweetB: Rule I use: a counter-trend rally retraces quickly. If $QQQ gives back half of Monday's 6.5% gap in under 3 sessions, the bears were right. If it holds, they're short into a 1998-style rally.

items.title: Burry vs Hayes vs Steno: three readings of the Jensen pop
items.idea: From Mando's 'Top Views': Michael Burry, 'NVDA is weaker, more craven than I thought'; Arthur Hayes, 'NVDA pump is the worst thing for crypto bags'; Andreas Steno, the chart 'says it's '98 not 2000, when semis rallied 602%.' Also: Peter Brandt (V-bottom unproven), Bob Loukas (stocks may have finished a deep 33-week cycle), Lyn Alden (BTC bottomed vs gold at the start of the Iran war).
items.angle: Hayes's view is the most tradeable: a revived AI trade takes marginal liquidity and attention away from crypto, and Monday's 19:1 Nasdaq/BTC capture (Lucky Trader) supports him.
items.tweetA: Steno says 1998, not 2000: semis rallied 602% from there. Burry says NVDA looks 'craven.' Both can be right. In 1998 the bubble got bigger even as governance got worse.
items.tweetB: Hayes: the NVDA pump is bad for crypto. Monday: Nasdaq +6.5%, BTC kept about a third of a percent. If AI is where the speculative money goes, crypto is now the funding source, not the risk-on trade that rides with it. $BTC

items.title: VIX -26%, its 7th-biggest one-day drop ever; NAAIM exposure 51, lowest since Apr 2025
items.idea: Chart of the Day (Charlie Bilello): VIX fell 26%, its 7th-biggest one-day drop. Separately, NAAIM manager exposure fell to 51, the lowest since April 2025. Brokers had outages as retail rushed in. Citadel: the '2018 playbook signals more market pain.' JPMorgan dropped its bullish view.
items.angle: A VIX crash with active managers only half invested means they hadn't chased the rally yet. If the price action holds, they're forced buyers. If it fails, they were right.
items.tweetA: The VIX fell 26% in a day while NAAIM managers are only 51% invested. Volatility sellers came back right away and active managers didn't. One of them is wrong, and the gap between them is where the next big move comes from. $VIX
items.tweetB: Citadel's flow desk is citing 2018. In 2018 the first violent relief rally (February) was followed by a retest. If this is the same pattern, the trade is selling volatility while still holding downside protection.

items.title: Arm's Rene Haas turned down the Nvidia CEO job; AMD registers 336.9M shares for potential sale
items.idea: AI & Tech headlines: Arm's Haas rejected the Nvidia CEO role. Jensen disclosed more affairs to the board and will testify publicly in the Senate next week. The US blacklisted Megaspeed and an Alibaba Singapore subsidiary. AMD registered 336.9M shares for potential sale. Marlowe raised $277M to rival Nvidia. Reports say Elon said SpaceX is falling behind on AI. Gemini 4 cut quantum-algorithm costs about 290x.
items.angle: The Haas refusal shows the board's succession options were thin, which helps explain the reversal. The AMD shelf registration in a rally is worth checking (likely a holder, possibly tied to OpenAI warrants).
items.tweetA: Before Nvidia brought Jensen back, Arm's Rene Haas reportedly turned the job down. When the best outside candidate says no, 'unanimous board confidence' sounds more like having no alternative. $NVDA $ARM
items.tweetB: $AMD registering 336.9M shares for potential sale during the biggest semis rally in history. Shelves get filed when the price is good. Find out whose shares these are before buying the sympathy rally.

items.title: Gemini 4 cuts quantum algorithm costs by about 290x; Claude claims a proof of VP ≠ VNP
items.idea: Two AI-for-science headlines: Google's Gemini 4 reportedly cut the cost of a quantum algorithm by about 290x, and Claude is credited with a claimed proof that VP ≠ VNP (the algebraic analogue of P vs NP). Together with Doomberg's Riemann item, that's three frontier math/physics claims in a week. The Ethereum Foundation (Lucky Trader) moved its post-quantum deadline to Dec 2028.
items.angle: A 290x cheaper quantum algorithm brings forward the date when quantum attacks matter for crypto. The Ethereum Foundation's earlier deadline is the first institutional reaction.
items.tweetA: Gemini 4 made a quantum algorithm about 290x cheaper. The Ethereum Foundation moved its post-quantum deadline to Dec 2028. AI is speeding up the quantum timeline, and the threat to crypto cryptography is getting closer. $ETH $BTC
items.tweetB: Three claims in one week: Riemann (Claude), VP ≠ VNP (Claude), 290x cheaper quantum algorithm (Gemini). Some will fail review. But the labs are now competing on research results, not just benchmark scores.

items.title: ECB will accept tokenised assets as collateral; South Korea ends its 2017 ICO ban; EU targets Russian crypto platforms
items.idea: Crypto regulation headlines: the ECB will accept tokenised assets as collateral; South Korea's crypto bill ends the 2017 ICO ban; the EU plans sanctions on Russian crypto platforms; the CFTC classed BTC, ETH and stables as 'financial resources'; BlackRock launched a tokenised MMF in Hong Kong; OKX-ICE launched despite objections from 90% of issuers; the DOJ moved to seize $1.1B from the Binance hack.
items.angle: The ECB accepting tokenised collateral is the biggest of these for market plumbing. A tokenised bond that can be posted at the central bank has the same value as the original, so the tokenisation discount goes away.
items.tweetA: The ECB will take tokenised assets as collateral. That sounds minor but it settles the question: if it can be posted at the central bank, it's money-like. The tokenised-vs-traditional spread goes to zero.
items.tweetB: Korea lifting its 2017 ICO ban during a crypto bear market fits a pattern: regulators open up when prices are low and nobody is euphoric. The opening comes before the next cycle, not with it.

items.angle: A record Beijing equity injection the same week the US tightened rental compute: China is supporting its tech stocks against export controls. Argentina going distressed again is the EM victim of the dollar's rally.
items.tweetA: Record CNY 90B state buying of Chinese stocks on Friday. The US Fed is hiking into a selloff and the White House rescued one company. China's state bought the whole index. Two very different ways of supporting a market. $FXI $KWEB
items.tweetB: Russia's nuclear-capable satellite, Iranian cyberattacks on 50 oil ships, Houthi strikes on Aramco: the energy-risk premium is building in space, cyber and Yemen while oil is down to $80.

items.title: BIS rental-compute rule: a license needed above about 760 H100s of Chinese access, plus licenses for 5 diversion countries
items.idea: The Nov 16 interim final rule (effective Nov 19) requires a license to supply Hopper/Blackwell chips to any overseas data center giving Chinese-parented firms more than about 760 H100-equivalents. Non-responsive KYC counts as a violation. It requires licenses for all advanced AI chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, and closes the Foundry Due-Diligence self-certification loophole. US-located data centers aren't covered yet. Treasury and the NSC wrote it, not Commerce.
items.angle: The FDD closure hits more than AI: per the FT, TSMC and Samsung have paused shipments to ByteDance, Baidu and Xiaomi. Phone-chip licence delays are a risk for China's smartphone supply chain.
items.tweetA: Under the new rule a Chinese company renting compute in Johor needs a license. Renting in Virginia doesn't, for now. US export controls currently cover data centers abroad but not at home.
items.tweetB: The overlooked part of the BIS rule is closing the Foundry Due-Diligence loophole. TSMC and Samsung have already paused shipments to ByteDance, Baidu and Xiaomi. That turns an AI export rule into a risk for Chinese smartphone supply chains. $TSM $1810.HK

items.title: A third of China's frontier-usable compute is rented abroad, about 1.2M H100-equivalents, roughly Anthropic's end-2025 compute
items.idea: ChinaTalk's new model: remote access is about a fifth of China's total compute but a third of frontier-usable compute (clusters over 2,000 chips), about 1.2M H100-equivalents, roughly what Anthropic had at end-2025. About 94% of the tracked overseas Chinese-tenant compute is in three Johor sites (DayOne Nusajaya and Kempas, Bridge's MY06). Will DePue finds six leading Chinese models carry a Blackwell fingerprint. ByteDance and Alibaba applied for 1.12M H200s for SE Asia, and BIS returned them all.
items.angle: A third of frontier-usable compute is about 1.2M H100e, which implies a total frontier pool of about 3.6M H100e. Johor is the chokepoint. DayOne/Bridge (Bain) tenant re-letting is the trade to watch.
items.tweetA: China's rented frontier compute is about 1.2M H100s, roughly Anthropic's entire end-2025 compute. 94% of it is in three buildings in Johor. Export control now comes down to whether a few buildings follow the rules.
items.tweetB: The fifth vs third gap tells you how it works: China can build lots of small domestic clusters, but its big training runs depend on rented Blackwells abroad. The rule targets exactly that.

charts.desc: 🔥 Model chart: China compute supply by source (domestic vs remote access), with rented share of frontier-usable compute

items.title: The 'commercial recommender' carve-out: DayOne gets 69% of revenue from a short-video giant
items.idea: The rule exempts compute used exclusively for 'commercial recommender systems' (rank/filter/suggest, not generate). DayOne runs the two largest Johor sites and 69% of its revenue comes from 'a global technology company with a leading short-form video platform', likely ByteDance. How 'exclusively' is read is up to BIS. Chris McGuire: if implemented broadly 'it could become a loophole you can drive a Mack truck through.'
items.angle: The carve-out is how the rule could end up toothless. Whether ByteDance's Johor clusters fall under the recommender exemption is the single biggest implementation question.
items.tweetA: One phrase in the BIS rule, 'exclusively for commercial recommender systems', could exempt the biggest Chinese compute tenant in Malaysia. 69% of DayOne's revenue comes from a short-video platform. How BIS interprets that phrase decides whether the rule works.
items.tweetB: Recommender or generator? Modern recommendation models are generative models. It's hard to prove a cluster is 'exclusively' ranking, so in practice the exemption gets decided by how much BIS trusts the tenant.

items.title: At 55% effective reach the rule delays China's frontier compute about 6 months by end-2028 (range 4-9)
items.idea: ChinaTalk's modelled delay: for every additional 10pp of rented compute actually stopped, China's frontier compute is delayed a bit over a month by end-2028. At their central effective-reach estimate of 55% (assuming BIS mostly denies licences), the median delay is about 6 months, with an interquartile range of 4-9 months. Leakage examples: Megaspeed (at least $7.5B of Nvidia chips, criminal probe) and Inspur's Aivres (over $5B of US tech sent to SE Asian centers serving Alibaba and ByteDance).
items.angle: Six months of compute lead matters most if you believe recursive self-improvement is close. For investors it means a policy lever worth about one model generation.
items.tweetA: Best case, the new BIS rule buys about six months of compute lead over China by 2028. Megaspeed alone bought $7.5B of Nvidia chips. Unless enforcement is real, the leakage will cancel the rule.
items.tweetB: Rule of thumb from the ChinaTalk model: each 10pp of China's rented compute actually blocked is worth about 1 month of US lead. So enforcement quality is what matters, not the rule text.

items.title: H100 rental prices are up about 55% since Dec 2025, and China's 'domestic chip share' rose mainly because total supply shrank
items.idea: Costs to US clouds look small: H100 rental prices are up about 55% since December 2025, freed clusters re-let within months, and a Malaysian operator re-let 68.4 MW from Megaspeed to Zenlayer. ChinaTalk puts forgone US operator revenue at about $1.5B a year. Domestic chips were 41% of China's AI accelerators in 2025 vs under 17% in 2023, but that ratio rose mostly because the denominator (total supply) shrank. Ascend volume went from under 1M to about 1.5M a year, and about 600k H200s sit in Hong Kong warehouses blocked by Beijing.
items.angle: A 55% rise in H100 rental prices since Dec 2025 shows a tight compute market. That supports CoreWeave, Nebius and other neoclouds and reduces the 'GPU glut' bear case.
items.tweetA: H100 rental prices are up about 55% since December 2025. People talk about a GPU glut, but rental prices say there's a shortage. Labs called to take Chinese tenants' capacity the day the rule came out. $CRWV $NBIS
items.tweetB: China's domestic AI chip share rose from 17% to 41%, which sounds like self-sufficiency. ChinaTalk's point: the share rose mostly because Nvidia supply fell, not because Huawei produced much more. Meanwhile 600k H200s sit in Hong Kong warehouses.

items.title: China's suspension of its gallium, germanium and antimony export ban to the US lapses Nov 27 unless renewed
items.idea: Most of the Busan-truce easing was extended to Jan 10, 2027, but the suspension of the gallium/germanium/antimony ban to the US still lapses on Nov 27, 2026 unless MOFCOM renews it. MOFCOM called the BIS rule a departure from the 'important consensus reached by the two heads of state' and threatened countermeasures. Huawei 950DT prices are up 20-50% on HBM shortages and SMIC ran at 97% utilisation in Q3. Possible retaliation targets: rare earths, batteries, optical interconnects, PCBs and other server components.
items.angle: Nov 27 is three days away. If it isn't renewed, that's China's retaliation without a new announcement: it just lets the suspension lapse. Gallium and germanium matter for defense electronics and compound semis. Optical interconnects are a risk for US AI buildout supply chains.
items.tweetA: China doesn't need to announce retaliation for the compute rule. It can just let the gallium/germanium/antimony suspension expire on Nov 27. Three days. Check who in your portfolio uses those minerals.
items.tweetB: ChinaTalk lists China's possible retaliation: rare earths, batteries, optical interconnects, PCBs and server components. Those are the inputs to the US AI buildout. Export controls on chips could be answered with controls on the parts that go around them.

items.title: BIS budget is $235M, against a $953bn one-day Nvidia move. Lutnick pushed a narrower rule
items.idea: The FY budget request nearly doubles BIS to $450M (about 290 more officials). The House agrees and the Senate recommends about $415M, up from $235M last year. The NYT reports Lutnick pushed a narrower version (notification only, seven countries) that would have spared a Malaysian center tied to a client of his family's firm. Axios says he stalled adding Megaspeed to the Entity List three times. Trump on CNBC: diversion through Megaspeed 'wouldn't be Jensen's fault,' and asked whether the stock drop influenced him, 'Probably so.'
items.angle: The enforcement agency is the bottleneck, and its leadership doesn't look committed. Assume weak enforcement unless BIS denies licences publicly.
items.tweetA: BIS's whole budget is $235M. Nvidia added $953bn of market cap on Monday. The agency policing the world's most valuable supply chain is funded at about 0.02% of one day's move in the stock it regulates.
items.tweetB: Asked whether Nvidia's stock drop influenced him, Trump said 'probably so.' So stock prices now help set export-control policy. That's a new input to model in semis.

items.title: Boockvar: in Jensen 2.0, the AI ecosystem gets less financing support from Nvidia
items.idea: Boockvar says NVDA's direction will depend on AI capex pace, what happens to its Asia business, and that 'the entire AI ecosystem has to assume that they will get less financing support from Nvidia in Jensen 2.0 than during Jensen's first term.' Nvidia is still a picks-and-shovels company.
items.angle: If Nvidia vendor financing pulls back (equity stakes, backstops, offtake deals), the weakest borrowers in the ecosystem (neoclouds, smaller labs) lose their cheapest funding at the same time the Fed is hiking.
items.tweetA: The question for Jensen 2.0 isn't the stock. It's whether Nvidia keeps acting as a lender to its own customers. Under congressional scrutiny, the circular financing slows. Neoclouds, look at your cost of capital. $NVDA $CRWV
items.tweetB: Melandri says the Jensen rally helps people who 'think circular financing is critical.' Boockvar says circular financing is about to shrink. If they're both right, Monday's rally was the circular-financing bulls' last good day.

items.title: HPE -11% premarket after +17% Monday and -19% the prior six days; it's still passing through commodity costs
items.idea: HPE fell 11% premarket on light guidance, after +17% Monday and -19% over the previous six sessions. Management: record backlog; orders driven by 'AI infrastructure spending in data center switching and routing'; 'significant double digit increases in commodities' in '26 which should moderate, and 'we will continue to pass those price increases through.' No change in order rates after the election, and 'an acceleration of AI in the enterprise.'
items.angle: Three moves of 10%+ in eight sessions on a large-cap hardware name shows how much volatility there is. Price pass-through is where memory/component inflation reaches enterprise IT budgets.
items.tweetA: -19%, +17%, -11% in eight sessions. That's HPE, a large-cap hardware company. A volatile, liquidating market is how things look after the crash, not only during it. $HPE
items.tweetB: HPE: 'we will continue to pass those price increases through.' Memory and commodity inflation are reaching enterprise server prices. Core goods inflation in tech hardware is something the Fed's model won't show until next year. $HPE $MU

items.title: Rosenberg's 'Jensen put': QQQ -1%, NVDA -4.8% overnight. 'The cat bounced, but it's still dead'
items.idea: Rosenberg calls the reinstatement a dangerous precedent of state capitalism and recommends the WSJ lead editorial 'Nvidia and Trump's State Capitalism', a critique of 'the quickest very thorough investigation in history.' US futures were back in the red overnight: QQQ down nearly 1%, NVDA -4.8%.
items.angle: The second day is the test. A 31% gain followed by -5% the next day is how bear-market rallies typically behave, and the governance discount is now being priced on top.
items.tweetA: Day 1: +31.5%. Day 2 premarket: -4.8%. When the government steps in to save a stock, it also has a say in what happens to it next. $NVDA now carries political risk on top of normal equity risk.
items.tweetB: 'Bull market in crony capitalism, bear market in corporate governance.' You can trade the first. The second gets priced slowly through lower multiples, as Chinese tech has shown for 5 years. $NVDA $KWEB

items.title: Melandri: 'AI is too big to fail' was the only thing holding the Fed back, and Monday removed it
items.idea: Harry Melandri (Respice Finem) called Monday a bear market rally: a 5% snap back after seven straight down days. He argues the only thing that would have stopped the Fed hiking was 'the AI trade getting broken... equity market dropping 10, 20 percent.' Monday removed that, so he sees a hike cycle running to March. Inflation has been above 2% 'for like 67 months in a row.' Underneath, meme stocks, BTC, private credit and BDCs are 'terrible.'
items.angle: This matches the FX Daily's 'Trump put gives the Fed room.' Two independent sources make the same point: the equity rescue tightens policy. Short the front end and favour quality over high beta.
items.tweetA: Inflation has been above 2% for 67 months. The only thing that might have stopped the Fed was an AI crash. On Monday the White House prevented the crash. The equity rescue may have raised the odds of a March hike.
items.tweetB: Underneath the record rally: meme stocks 'awful,' BTC weak, private credit and BDCs 'terrible.' AI is the only strong part of the market. That's not a healthy rally. One sector is carrying the whole market.

items.title: The 'dead parrot' housing market lets the Fed keep hiking; Florida weak, Long Island strongest
items.idea: Melandri: housing transactions are 'almost completely dead' outside the Tri-State area, so further hikes do little extra damage there. A dead housing market gives the Fed cover to keep going. Regionally, Florida is the worst (insurance costs keep rising), Long Island is 'probably the strongest market in the US,' and New England 'people don't understand how bad they are yet.' Mando: US homebuyer demand is at a record low.
items.angle: Normally weak housing is what makes the Fed stop. When transactions are already near zero, that channel stops working, so rates can stay higher for longer. Bearish for homebuilders in Florida and for Sun Belt regional banks.
items.tweetA: Normally weak housing makes the Fed stop hiking. Melandri: housing transactions are already near zero, so another hike barely hurts. A dead market can't send a stop signal. Rates stay higher than the models assume.
items.tweetB: The US housing market splits three ways: Long Island strongest in the country, Florida hurt by insurance costs, New England 'doesn't know how bad it is yet.' Insurance, not mortgage rates, is now driving regional prices. $LEN $DHI

items.title: Melandri: if Iranian tankers trying to run the blockade are sunk, expect retaliation on Saudi/Gulf infrastructure, and that isn't priced
items.idea: Melandri: 'The Islamic Republic and its leadership is trapped' and won't go 'gently into that good night.' Iran plans to push tankers through the US naval blockade (Mando: 'Iran plans to confront US naval blockade'). If they are sunk, he expects retaliation on Saudi and Gulf infrastructure, which 'we're not seeing reflected in prices.' On Russia, his working hypothesis is that Putin has been discredited and hardliners are in control, driving the strikes on Ukrainian energy.
items.angle: Combine this with Doomberg's Houthi strikes on Aramco and PIF. Two independent sources point to Saudi infrastructure as the exposed target this winter, while oil is under $80.
items.tweetA: Iran says it will push tankers through the blockade. If the US sinks them, the obvious retaliation targets are Saudi Arabia and the Gulf, which the Houthis are already hitting. Oil is $80 and falling. I don't think that adds up. $XLE $USO
items.tweetB: Melandri's view is that Putin has been sidelined by hardliners, which explains the escalating strikes on Ukrainian energy. If that's right, peace-talk headlines (Merz) are less meaningful, and Europe's gas risk premium shouldn't be fading.

items.title: 19:1: Nasdaq kept 6.5% of the Jensen catalyst, Bitcoin kept almost none, and ETFs sold $570M into the bounce
items.idea: BTC touched $63,929 (+5.1%) Monday and finished near $61k, barely up; it's now $60.1k. The Nasdaq closed +6.51% at 24,089. That's a 19:1 ratio on the same catalyst. Spot BTC ETFs had $569M net outflows and ETH ETFs $85M. Crypto fell with AI stocks all the way down, then didn't follow them back up, so the shared-liquidity explanation failed its test.
items.angle: Crypto rises with tech on the way down but not on the way up. That's how a funding source behaves (sold to raise cash), not how a risk asset behaves. Until ETF flows turn, rallies get sold.
items.tweetA: Same catalyst, same day: Nasdaq +6.5%, Bitcoin about +0.3%. ETFs sold $570M into the bounce. If crypto falls with tech but doesn't rise with it, it's being sold to raise cash, not held as risk-on. $BTC $IBIT
items.tweetB: Lucky Trader puts it at 19:1. Vanda says retail sold other holdings to fund NVDA. That explains it: retail sold crypto to buy Nvidia, so the AI rally pulled money out of BTC.

items.title: NVDA shorts lost $12.2B in a day, more than the $10.5B they made the prior week; December 50bp hike odds fell to 0%
items.idea: Short sellers took about $12.2B in paper losses on Monday, their worst day since at least 2019, wiping out the $10.5B made the prior week. Huang's net worth rose about $36.6B on his 3.5% stake. CME FedWatch odds of a 50bp December hike went to 0% (from about 10% ten days ago). Futures this morning: Dow -0.5%, Nasdaq -1.9%; Anthropic ('ANT') is below its IPO price.
items.angle: When shorts give back a week's profit in one day, the next downtrend starts with fewer shorts to cover, so the falls are less cushioned. ANT below IPO is a sentiment signal for the AI-IPO pipeline.
items.tweetA: NVDA shorts made $10.5B in a week, then lost $12.2B in a day. Shorting a stock the government is willing to rescue has asymmetric risk, and shorts will be smaller from now on. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Buried in the note: Anthropic is trading below its IPO price this morning. In a week with a claimed Claude Riemann proof and a record AI rally, the newest AI IPO is underwater. Public markets aren't paying for AI research results.

items.title: Strategy owns 851,305 BTC at a $75,446 average, about $12.1B underwater; it moved $1B out of its USD Reserve
items.idea: Strategy bought 457 BTC ($29.6M at $64,898) and moved $1B from its USD Reserve into a general cash account, leaving 851,305 BTC carried at $75,446 each, about $12.1B underwater (Lucky Trader). Unchained: it raised its preferred (STRC) buyback to $4B from $3B after repurchasing $211.8M last week. BitMine holds 6,085,564 ETH (4.98% of supply), about 3 weeks from its 5% target.
items.angle: Moving reserve cash to general cash plus a bigger preferred buyback means they're managing the preferred-stock structure, not buying BTC. A $12B unrealised loss on a company whose only business is holding BTC is the most-watched number in crypto.
items.tweetA: $MSTR: 851,305 BTC at a $75,446 cost basis, BTC at $60k. About $12B underwater, and the $1B USD Reserve just became 'general cash.' Watch where that cash goes: BTC, the preferred buyback, or dividends.
items.tweetB: BitMine owns 4.98% of all ETH and will reach 5% in about three weeks. One company holding 1 in 20 ETH: is that adoption or concentration risk? The ETH ETFs' $85M outflow Monday suggests the market sees it as concentration risk. $BMNR $ETH

items.title: Bitcoin printed C$24,250 (about $17k), 70% below global prices on Kraken's CAD book, and Kraken says the trades stand
items.idea: Early Saturday, BTC traded as low as C$24,250 (about US$17,000) on Kraken's Canadian-dollar book, about 70% below global prices across 976 trades in 15 minutes. Kraken said every order executed properly and the trades stand. Also: ARK withdrew its CoinDesk 20 and CoinDesk 20 ex-BTC ETFs ten months after filing.
items.angle: A 70% flash crash on a major venue's thin fiat pair shows how thin weekend crypto liquidity is. It's an argument for limit orders and against stop-market orders on smaller order books.
items.tweetA: BTC traded at about $17k on Kraken's CAD book Saturday, 976 trades in 15 minutes, and the trades stand. If you use stop-market orders on thin fiat pairs, this is the risk. On weekends crypto liquidity is much thinner than it looks.
items.tweetB: ARK withdrew two crypto index ETFs ten months after filing. When a firm that markets itself on crypto drops its own products, crypto ETF demand outside BTC/ETH looks weak.

items.title: Ethereum Foundation brings its post-quantum deadline forward to Dec 2028, calling AI-driven bug-finding the more urgent threat
items.idea: The Ethereum Foundation doubled its protocol security team and moved its post-quantum deadline to December 2028. Researcher Kev Wedderburn said AI-driven vulnerability discovery is more urgent than quantum. Lucky Trader thinks crypto's next catalyst is 'likely quantum-related' and probably not in 2026.
items.angle: The EF says AI attacking smart contracts is a bigger near-term threat than quantum computers. Expect DeFi exploit frequency to rise and audit/insurance protocols to gain value.
items.tweetA: The Ethereum Foundation says AI finding vulnerabilities is more urgent than quantum. Every exposed smart contract can now be scanned by models that improve monthly. DeFi's security budget has to go up. $ETH
items.tweetB: Post-quantum deadline: Dec 2028. Gemini 4 just made a quantum algorithm about 290x cheaper. The EF can move deadlines; Bitcoin's governance is much slower to change. Quantum readiness may become a selling point for ETH over BTC.

items.title: A Pump.fun memecoin for Fiona the hippo has sent $103,600 to the Cincinnati Zoo
items.idea: A Pump.fun token honoring Fiona the Cincinnati Zoo hippo has sent about $103,600 to the Zoological Society of Cincinnati by routing 100% of creator rewards to the charity. FIONA was +100% among Solana top movers. Also: Ansem's pump wallet appears hacked (ANSEM -50%), and Hyperliquid led on-chain protocol revenue at $3.85M/day.
items.angle: Charity-routed creator fees are a new memecoin model where the 'creator' is a cause. It may become a recurring fundraising channel, and a regulatory headache.
items.tweetA: A hippo memecoin has raised $103k for a zoo through creator fees. Charitable funding has a new channel: a speculative token sends its trading fees to a cause. Expect regulators and the IRS to look at it within a year.
items.tweetB: Hyperliquid made $3.85M in one day, Pump.fun $1.35M, and a zoo $103k from a hippo token. Crypto is in a bear market and on-chain casino revenue is still high. Speculation didn't stop, it moved to these platforms.

items.title: DOJ seeks the $1.1B in USDC stolen by North Korea, and Circle has agreed to mint replacement USDC for the government
items.idea: The DOJ filed civil forfeiture for over $1.1B in USDC that North Korean hackers stole from Binance around Oct 29 (frozen under a Nov 12 order). Circle agreed to issue new USDC equal to the restrained amount and hand it to the government if a judge orders forfeiture. The case is part of an effort to help Binance recover over $6B in stolen assets.
items.angle: The issuer can neutralise stolen tokens and reissue them to the state. That's a precedent: USDC works like a bank deposit with a central ledger and a court-order process, not like cash.
items.tweetA: Circle will mint new USDC to replace what North Korea stole, if a judge orders it. Stablecoins aren't bearer cash. They're bank deposits with a court-order process. Good for compliance, bad if you thought you held cash. $CRCL
items.tweetB: $1.1B frozen and reissuable by court order. Tether hasn't done anything comparable. Circle's ability to cooperate with US courts like this is its main selling point to institutions. Distribution matters, but this is the edge over Tether in regulated markets.

items.title: Sky cofounder: 'This is on me.' His 77M USDS of loans are about half of what stUSDS depositors can't withdraw
items.idea: Rune Christensen said his own borrowing is 'part of why stUSDS can't withdraw today.' He repaid 3M USDS and still owes about 77M USDS against staked SKY. Depositor claims total 158.7M USDS and depositors can only withdraw what isn't lent out; one says they've been stuck 'for over a week.' He may sell SKY to institutions, and Du Jun (Vernal) wants the whole position. The Uneasy Money preview notes $2B in USDS redemptions and caution flags on Upbit/Bithumb.
items.angle: Math: 77M of 158.7M is about 49% of the locked pool owed by the founder alone. It's an insider-concentration run on a DeFi credit product, during a $2B redemption wave.
items.tweetA: Sky's stUSDS pool: 158.7M USDS of depositor claims. The cofounder owes 77M of it, about 49%. Depositors have been stuck for a week. That's a founder borrowing from his own users. $SKY
items.tweetB: $2B in USDS redemptions, a founder loan blocking withdrawals, and Korean exchange warnings. The yield-stablecoin model has the same problem as a bank: depositors can leave instantly, but the assets backing them can't be sold that fast.

items.title: OKXICE tokenized stocks launch, but 67 companies opted out, including Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla
items.idea: OKX and ICE's tokenized-stock venue went live Monday with six USDC-paired stocks (incl. Coinbase, Circle, Robinhood), each backed 1:1 with a real share and passing through dividends and votes. Trades settle on Uniswap v4 pools on OKX's X Layer, for vetted US customers only. The pipeline is 113 names, but 67 companies objected under the SEC Innovation Exemption, which lets a company keep its stock off the venue if it objects within 30 days.
items.angle: Issuer opt-out is the real limit on tokenized equities. The mega-caps said no, so the venue will mostly list crypto-adjacent names, which limits volume.
items.tweetA: Tokenized US stocks are live on Uniswap pools. 67 companies, including $AAPL $MSFT $NVDA $TSLA, said no. Whether a stock trades on-chain now depends on its issuer. That's a permissioned system built on permissionless rails.
items.tweetB: The SEC Innovation Exemption gives issuers a veto. The companies that opt in will be crypto-friendly ones ($COIN $HOOD $CRCL). The on-chain stock market will end up concentrated in crypto-related names, not a broad market.

items.title: CFTC staff: BTC/ETH can cover up to half of a clearinghouse's reserve with a 20% haircut, stablecoins 2%
items.idea: CFTC staff guidance says bitcoin and ether can count toward up to half of a futures exchange's or clearinghouse's one-year operating-expense reserve with a 20% haircut, and payment stablecoins with a 2% haircut. It's staff guidance, not a formal rule. The CFTC also finalized a rule requiring prediction markets to collect trader name, address, occupation and employer. Chairman Selig: no more 'patchwork of no-action letters.'
items.angle: A 2% stablecoin haircut puts payment stables close to cash for regulatory capital, a first for US derivatives plumbing. Prediction-market KYC adds friction that could slow Kalshi/Polymarket retail growth.
items.tweetA: CFTC haircuts: BTC 20%, ETH 20%, payment stablecoins 2%. US derivatives regulators now treat stablecoins as close to cash for clearinghouse capital. That changes stablecoins' role in market plumbing. $CRCL
items.tweetB: Prediction markets now have to collect your employer and occupation. The anonymity is gone. The interesting use case: insider-trading enforcement on event contracts can now trace trades back to where people work.

items.title: Kalshi pauses new trades for 177,000+ Utah users after state criminal charges
items.idea: Kalshi paused new trades for its more than 177,000 Utah users amid criminal charges from the state; they can only close positions and withdraw. In New York, Justice Melissa Crane signaled she'll deny the AG's TRO and expedite an injunction hearing, citing the year-long status quo.
items.angle: Federal CFTC approval vs state gambling law is turning into a criminal fight in Utah. State-by-state geofencing is the operational risk for every prediction-market valuation.
items.tweetA: 177,000 Kalshi users in one small state, now limited to closing positions under criminal charges. Prediction markets have a federal regulator and 50 state gambling regulators. Price in the state risk. $HOOD
items.tweetB: Utah: criminal charges. New York: the judge declines to halt Kalshi. The same product is treated very differently from state to state, which usually ends at the Supreme Court. Prediction markets will run on legal uncertainty for years.

items.title: Japan found ¥3.9B of undeclared crypto income from 90 people and joins CARF data sharing in 2027
items.idea: Tokyo's regional tax bureau found more than ¥3.9B (about $24.5M) in undeclared crypto income from roughly 90 users last fiscal year. Japan will strengthen audits and from 2027 exchange crypto transaction data with foreign tax authorities under the OECD Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF).
items.angle: That's about ¥43M ($270k) undeclared per person. When CARF takes effect, offshore exchange accounts stop being invisible, and some holders may sell before 2027.
items.tweetA: Japan: ¥3.9B of undeclared crypto income from 90 people, about $270k each. From 2027 CARF shares crypto data across borders. For most holders, offshore exchanges stop hiding anything in 13 months.
items.tweetB: CARF is crypto's version of the 2017 CRS for bank accounts. After CRS, offshore deposits were repatriated or declared within about two years. Expect the same for crypto, with some selling to pay back taxes.

items.title: Visa launches an agent-wallet CLI: verified AI agents complete paid tasks and earn OUSD on Tempo
items.idea: Visa launched an experimental agent wallet CLI for US users that lets AI agents verified through its Trusted Agent Protocol complete paid tasks and earn OUSD. It runs on Tempo (Stripe's chain) and the Machine Payments Protocol. Also: BlackRock launched its first tokenized money fund in Hong Kong, subscribable with HKDAP, a licensed stablecoin.
items.angle: Visa is building identity and payment for AI agents on a stablecoin chain. Card networks want to be the trust layer for agent payments, not get bypassed. Notable that it's Tempo and not Base.
items.tweetA: Visa is building wallets for AI agents to earn stablecoins on Stripe's chain. Card networks have decided the threat isn't crypto replacing them, it's agents not needing them. So they're getting in early. $V
items.tweetB: AI agents completing paid tasks and getting paid in OUSD. If agents earn and spend in stablecoins, who books the revenue, the person, the agent, or the protocol? Accounting standards haven't caught up.

items.title: American Bitcoin borrows $150M from FalconX at 143% collateral; a 2x Zcash ETF falls 13% on day one
items.idea: Eric Trump-backed miner American Bitcoin secured a $150M FalconX credit facility backed by its BTC at an initial 143% collateral ratio and a 5.95% loan fee. Grayscale's 2x leveraged Zcash ETF (ZECX) fell 13% on its first NYSE Arca day to $28.63. DeFi Development added 5,180 SOL (11th straight week, about 2.62M SOL). Strive bought nothing, and its cash dipped $2.9M to $462.4M.
items.angle: Miners borrowing against BTC at 143% collateral with BTC at $60k: a drop of about 30% from here triggers margin calls. Leverage in crypto treasuries is building in the bear market.
items.tweetA: Miner borrows $150M against BTC at 143% collateral. At a $60k entry, liquidation risk starts around $42k. In 2022 this was the setup for forced selling in the bear market. $ABTC
items.tweetB: A 2x leveraged Zcash ETF fell 13% on day one. Leveraged single-coin ETFs on small caps keep launching, which shows issuers think there's demand. In a bear market, the fact that this product exists says more than its first-day return.
